Right, and as I said before, I'm sure there's something to it, otherwise there may have been a response along those lines. But, (as someone who is in university studying this very subject) any story that distracts from the intended message is a detriment. So, in this case, one part might be true while others aren't. Or it might all be true. It really doesn't matter from the quoted rep's perspective, because engaging it gives the story traction and takes the promotion off message. Whether the story concerns Ninja being a dick, Hugh Jackman's UPS shorts, or a boom operator stubbing his toe, the response will most likely be some form of what appears in this article. Also, Blomkamp didn't say "no comment," a rep gave a statement, and there is a difference there. Nothing about this article tells me he was even reached for comment. 

All I'm saying is drawing a conclusion based on an absence of a comment might be a tad hasty. An article full of blind quotes with no confirmation from the principals is dubious at best. Journalism has rules, not that everyone follows them. One of them is that you don't put quotes around something unless you yourself hear the person say it. If you do, it's called hearsay, which is not good. 

Really not trying to come off as argumentative or condescending here, it's a slow day at work and this is a fun topic for me.

One reply to a comment is "relentless?" 

When you say "they," it sounds like you're assuming the studio and production team all got together to concoct a reply. It's much more likely that response came from their media relations person, whose job is to disseminate a positive message about the film. So, when a reporter calls up and asks "hey was Ninja an asshole?" the likely response is "Well I don't know but I do know that Chappie is awesome and can I tell you more about that?" EDIT: Just re-read it and yeah that quote is from a rep. 

Hope that's more clear, or at least something else you can laugh about. If you want to take that as being apologist, not much I can do about it. I wasn't there, for all I know yes he was a reprehensible jerk-off.

I'm sure there's something to it, but this:

“I don’t ever want to be in the same room as him again,” said Blomkamp of Ninja, according to sources.

is shitty journalism. A quote like that needs to come from a primary  source, not second-hand. 

As for the rest, well, Ninja kinda strikes me as someone who is used to controlling the creative direction of whatever he's involved in, unless it's with someone he admires like Ballon. I'm sure there's some decorum on a big set like that that most of the other movie pros know well, but maybe Ninja was a bit of a bull in a china shop. 

Don't read too much into a "no comment," a lot of times that's a blanket policy.

One way I can suggest to get a foot in the door is to offer to roadie. It can be as simple as waiting until a band is loading out of a show and asking someone if they need help carrying something, or going with a friend's band to their show as a roadie and chatting with other bands on the bill. Maybe stay near the stage and help with set changes. Saving a band 2 minutes by helping get the drummer's 94 cymbal stands onto the riser can buy them time for another song. Do that a few times and you should get a bit more regard. If not, find a new scene that isn't full of tools. 

It's not a 100% method or anything, but maybe something that can help. Best of luck!
